DABAANG in Telugu

The 1989 Malayalam film “Vadakkunokkiyanthram”, which won Thilakan and Srinivasan a National Award each, is back again. After the film was remade in Hindi as “Saat Uchakkey” last year, it’s making its presence felt in a roundabout way in Telugu too.

The Telugu film “Motor Venuka Taka” , directed by debutant K. Lakshmiprasad, has its central character pining over a girl who matches the description of a certain character in “Vadakkunokkiyanthram”. But the one doing the pining in the Telugu film is not someone like Ganesh (Sreenivasan) from the original but a woman. There is also no doppelganger angle in the remake. The heroine, deserves credit for sensibly reworking the theme.

Like the young man Aravind Menon in “Vadakkunokkiyanthram” , Rani, played by Anisha Rane, is a loser in love. She tries to project the image of a successful woman with a well-paid job and a comfortable life around her mother and other family members, even while her heart still yearns for her college sweetheart. Her mask starts to slip when the young man, Karthik (Venu), (Venu Gopal), returns to her life.

In between there is the tale of a young married couple trying to come to terms with life’s harsh realities. A climax that sees almost all the characters from “Vadakkunokkiyanthram” make a comeback in either a changed avatar, or in the role of characters from the original script. Anisha Rane plays her character well, giving an interesting twist to the character Mohanalal essayed in the original. The young woman plays the character of a lovelorn heroine, saddled with a string of failures in her quest to meet an ideal she never believed could exist. Meanwhile, Gandhi’s daughter Jyothi, who is making her debut in films, plays Rani’s beloved friend, Aasritha, who comes across as stronger character in this version. Avinash, Pooja Ramachandran, Surya and M.S. Narayana fill out the rest of the cast.

Composer R.R. Doss has scored the music, and cinematographer B. Rajashekar handled the cinematography. A decent remake in its own right, “Motor Venuka Taka” fails to leave a mark on the audience. But it deserves a pat on the back for giving the director a chance to prove her talent.
